_comment: Labelled retrieval golden set for ContextFlow.
The domain is DELIBERATELY FICTIONAL. If the corpus described real-world
software, a model could answer from prior knowledge and both retrieval and
faithfulness scores would be inflated by facts that never came from the
context. 'Meridian' exists only in this file, so an answer is either
grounded in retrieved context or invented.
Relevance is labelled by (document, marker substring) rather than by chunk
id, because chunk ids are assigned at ingest and chunk boundaries move
whenever the chunker changes. A chunk counts as relevant when it belongs to
the named document AND contains the marker, case-insensitively.
PHASE 3 EXPANSION. Phase 5 measured MRR 1.000 at every k on the original
six-document corpus and concluded it was too easy to discriminate between
retrieval strategies: it would catch a regression but could never show that
a reranker helps. The ten documents added here are built as NEAR-MISS
DISTRACTORS rather than as more subject matter:
- Four documents now describe a 'rotation' (workspace token, encryption
key, on-call shift, log file). They share almost all surface vocabulary
and answer completely different questions.
- 'retained for N' appears with six different values of N across six
documents (14 days, 30 days, 90 days, 180 days, 400 days, 1 year,
7 years). Retrieving the right retention window now requires reading
the query, not matching the phrase.
- Quota (a limit at rest) and rate limit (a limit on speed) are separate
documents that each explicitly disclaim the other.
- Support response targets and incident severities are separate documents
that both discuss urgency and both use the word 'severity'.
- A CLI error-code reference supplies identifier queries (E1042, E4021),
which dense retrieval is structurally bad at and the sparse arm exists
for.
This is what makes 'measurable recall@k and nDCG improvement' a real exit
criterion rather than a formality on a set that already scores 1.000.

documents.title: Meridian Deployment Runbook
documents.text:
# Meridian Deployment Runbook

## Release Channels

Meridian ships through three release channels. The canary channel receives every merged commit and serves two percent of production traffic. The stable channel receives promotions from canary after a soak period of six hours with no elevated error rate. The pinned channel never advances automatically and exists for customers on the Anchored support tier, who upgrade on a schedule they control.

A release is identified by a Meridian release tag, which is the build date followed by a two-letter sequence code, for example 20260714-af. Release tags are immutable once published. Rebuilding the same commit produces a new tag rather than overwriting the old one, because the pinned channel may still be serving the previous artifact.

## Rollback Procedure

To roll back a bad deploy, run the meridian rollback command with the previous release tag. The rollback command restores the previous container image, drains in-flight connections over a thirty second window, and then swaps the routing table. Rollback does not revert database migrations. If the bad release included a forward-incompatible migration, roll back the application first and then apply the inverse migration manually using the migration console.

Rollback is blocked automatically when the target release tag is older than fourteen days, because artifacts older than that are garbage collected from the registry. Rolling back to an evicted artifact fails with a registry miss. To roll back further than fourteen days, first restore the artifact from cold storage using the artifact restore command, which takes roughly eight minutes.

## Health Checks

The readiness probe queries the primary database, the graph store, and the object cache. A failing readiness probe removes the instance from the load balancer rotation but does not terminate it, so that a wedged instance can still be inspected. The liveness probe checks only that the process is responsive, and a failing liveness probe restarts the container after three consecutive failures thirty seconds apart.

During a deploy, readiness failures are expected while connections drain. The deploy controller therefore suppresses readiness alerts for the first ninety seconds after a routing table swap.

documents.title: Meridian Billing Policy
documents.text:
# Meridian Billing Policy

## Plans

Meridian offers three plans. Starter is billed monthly at a flat rate and includes one workspace. Team is billed monthly or annually and includes up to twenty workspaces. Anchored is billed annually only, includes unlimited workspaces, and carries the pinned release channel.

## Refunds

Refunds are issued within fourteen days of the billing date for annual plans. Monthly plans are not refundable once the billing date has passed, but a monthly plan can be cancelled at any time and will remain active until the end of the paid period. A refund on an annual plan is prorated against whole months consumed, not days.

Refund requests are processed by the billing service within two business days. A refund that fails to process automatically is escalated to a billing operator, who may issue an account credit instead if the original payment method is no longer valid.

## Overage

Workspace overage on the Team plan is billed at the end of the cycle rather than blocking creation, so a burst of workspace creation never interrupts work. Overage charges appear as a separate line item and are not eligible for the fourteen day refund window, because they represent consumption that already occurred.

## Invoices

Invoices are generated on the billing date and retained for seven years for tax purposes. An invoice can be reissued with corrected billing details, which produces a superseding invoice rather than editing the original. The original remains retrievable through the invoice history endpoint.

documents.title: Meridian Authentication
documents.text:
# Meridian Authentication

## Token Types

Meridian issues three token types. A session token is short lived and is used by the web console; it expires after thirty minutes of inactivity. A workspace token is scoped to a single workspace and is used by automation; it expires after ninety days and can be rotated without downtime by issuing the replacement before revoking the original. A service token is scoped to the whole account, never expires, and may only be created by an account owner.

Service tokens are the highest risk credential in Meridian. They are displayed exactly once at creation and are stored only as a hash, so a lost service token cannot be recovered and must be replaced.

## Rotation

Workspace token rotation is a two step process. First issue a replacement token, which produces a second valid credential for the same workspace. Then update the consumers and revoke the original. Both tokens are valid during the overlap, which may last up to seven days; after seven days the original is revoked automatically whether or not it is still in use.

## Failed Authentication

Five consecutive failed authentication attempts against the same account lock the account for fifteen minutes. The lock applies to interactive sign in only and does not affect workspace or service tokens, because locking automation out during a credential problem tends to turn an incident into an outage. Failed attempts are recorded in the audit log with the source address but never with the attempted credential.

documents.title: Meridian Data Retention
documents.text:
# Meridian Data Retention

## Retention Windows

Meridian retains different classes of data for different periods. Audit log entries are retained for four hundred days. Application logs are retained for thirty days. Deleted workspaces are held in a recoverable state for sixty days before being purged, during which an account owner can restore them in full.

Invoices are excluded from these windows and are retained for seven years, which is a tax requirement rather than a product decision.

## Deletion Requests

A verified deletion request removes account data within thirty days. Backups are excluded from the thirty day window and age out on their own ninety day cycle, so data may persist in backup for up to ninety days after a deletion request completes. This is disclosed at request time rather than discovered afterwards.

Deletion does not remove aggregate usage counters, because they contain no identifying information and are required for capacity planning.

## Export

An account owner can export all workspace content at any time. The export is produced asynchronously and is available for seven days as a single archive. Exports are rate limited to one per account per twenty four hours, because generating one reads the full workspace history.

documents.title: Meridian API Rate Limits
documents.text:
# Meridian API Rate Limits

## Limits by Token Type

Rate limits in Meridian are applied per token, not per account, so one noisy automation cannot starve the rest of an account. A session token is limited to sixty requests per minute. A workspace token is limited to six hundred requests per minute. A service token is limited to three thousand requests per minute.

Limits are enforced with a sliding window rather than a fixed bucket, so a client cannot double its effective rate by straddling a window boundary.

## Exceeding a Limit

Exceeding a rate limit returns a rate limited response with a retry after header giving the number of seconds until capacity is available. Clients should honour the retry after value rather than retrying immediately; repeated immediate retries against a limited token extend the window rather than resetting it.

A token that exceeds its limit continuously for more than one hour is flagged for review, and an account owner is notified. The token is not revoked automatically, because an automatic revocation during a traffic spike would convert a performance problem into an outage.

## Increases

Rate limit increases are available on the Team and Anchored plans and are applied per token type. An increase request requires a description of the workload, because the limits exist to protect shared capacity and an increase is granted against a specific expected pattern.

documents.title: Meridian Incident Response
documents.text:
# Meridian Incident Response

## Severity Levels

Meridian classifies incidents into three severities. A severity one incident is a full outage or a confirmed data exposure and pages the on call engineer immediately. A severity two incident is a partial degradation affecting more than ten percent of requests and pages during business hours only. A severity three incident is a defect with a workaround and is triaged on the next working day.

Severity is set by the first responder and can be raised by anyone, but can only be lowered by the incident commander, so that pressure to close an incident cannot quietly downgrade it.

## Declaring an Incident

An incident is declared with the meridian incident declare command, which opens a channel, pages according to severity, and starts the timeline. The timeline is append only. Every subsequent status update is recorded against it, and the timeline becomes the basis of the review.

## Review

Every severity one and severity two incident gets a written review within five working days. The review is blameless and focuses on the conditions that allowed the failure rather than on the person who triggered it. A review that identifies no action items is acceptable and is sometimes the correct outcome, but it must say so explicitly rather than leaving the section empty.

documents.title: Meridian Encryption Key Rotation
documents.text:
# Meridian Encryption Key Rotation

## Rotation Schedule

Meridian rotates the data encryption key for each workspace every ninety days. Rotation is automatic and requires no action from an account owner. A rotation event re-encrypts the workspace key envelope under the new key version; it does not re-encrypt stored objects, which continue to reference the key version they were written under.

Key rotation is entirely separate from credential rotation. Rotating an encryption key does not invalidate any token, and rotating a token does not trigger a key rotation. Conflating the two is the most common source of confusion in support requests.

## Manual Rotation

An account owner on the Anchored plan may force an out of cycle key rotation from the security console. A forced rotation is rate limited to one per workspace per twenty four hours, because each rotation writes a new key envelope for every object prefix in the workspace.

Forced rotation does not cause downtime and does not interrupt in-flight requests. Old key versions are retained for one hundred and eighty days so that objects written under them remain readable, after which any object still referencing an expired key version is re-wrapped by a background job.

## Compromise

If a key version is believed to be compromised, open a severity one incident rather than using the self service rotation. A compromise response revokes the key version immediately instead of retaining it, which requires the re-wrap job to complete before the affected objects are readable again. That job takes roughly four hours per terabyte.

documents.title: Meridian On-Call Rotation
documents.text:
# Meridian On-Call Rotation

## Schedule

The Meridian on call rotation runs weekly and hands over on Wednesday at ten hundred local time. Each rotation has a primary and a secondary responder. The secondary is paged only when the primary does not acknowledge within five minutes.

A responder may swap a shift with another responder without approval, provided the swap is recorded before the handover. Unrecorded swaps are the most common cause of an unacknowledged page, because the paging system routes on the recorded schedule rather than on the intended one.

## Paging

Paging is driven by incident severity and not by the on call schedule itself. A severity one incident pages the primary immediately at any hour. A severity two incident pages during business hours in the responder's local timezone. A severity three incident never pages and appears in the next working day triage queue.

If neither primary nor secondary acknowledges within fifteen minutes, the page escalates to the engineering manager on the escalation list. Escalation is logged against the incident timeline.

## Handover

Every handover produces a written note listing open incidents, suppressed alerts, and any deploy freeze in effect. A deploy freeze declared during a shift survives the handover and must be lifted explicitly; it does not expire when the shift ends.

documents.title: Meridian Support Tiers and Response Times
documents.text:
# Meridian Support Tiers and Response Times

## Tiers

Meridian offers three support tiers. Standard support is included with the Starter and Team plans. Priority support is available as an add on to the Team plan. Anchored support is included with the Anchored plan and carries the pinned release channel.

## Response Targets

A support response target is the time to a first human response, not the time to resolution. Standard support targets one business day for all requests. Priority support targets four business hours for urgent requests and one business day otherwise. Anchored support targets one hour for urgent requests, at any hour, and four business hours otherwise.

A support response target is not an incident severity. Severity classifies the impact of a production failure and drives paging; a support target describes how quickly a written request is answered. A severity two incident and an urgent support request are unrelated things that happen to both feel urgent.

## Escalation

A support request that misses its response target is escalated automatically to the support lead. An account owner may also escalate a request manually once per request. Manual escalation does not reset the response target clock, which continues to run from the original request time.

## Exclusions

Support targets do not apply to feature requests, to requests about code the customer wrote against the API, or to requests submitted through the community forum rather than the support console.

documents.title: Meridian Workspace Quotas
documents.text:
# Meridian Workspace Quotas

## Quota Types

A quota limits how much of a resource a workspace may hold at rest. This is different from a rate limit, which limits how fast requests may be made. Exceeding a quota blocks the write that would exceed it; exceeding a rate limit delays requests but never rejects stored data.

Each workspace has a storage quota of five hundred gigabytes, a document quota of two million documents, and an attachment size limit of one hundred megabytes per file.

## Exceeding a Quota

A write that would exceed a storage or document quota is rejected with a quota exceeded response, and the workspace enters a read only state for writes of that resource type. Reads, exports, and deletions continue to work, because a workspace that cannot delete data cannot recover from a full quota.

Quota state is evaluated at write time rather than continuously, so a workspace that drops below its quota through deletion becomes writable again on the next write attempt without any manual reset.

## Increases

Quota increases are requested through the support console and are reviewed rather than granted automatically, because storage quota is backed by provisioned capacity. Rate limit increases follow a different process and are described in the rate limit documentation.

Quota increases are not available on the Starter plan. A Starter workspace at its quota must either delete data or move to the Team plan.

documents.title: Meridian Database Migrations
documents.text:
# Meridian Database Migrations

## Forward Migrations

A Meridian migration is identified by a migration id, which is a four digit sequence followed by a short slug, for example 0142-add-workspace-index. Migration ids are allocated at merge time and are never reused.

Migrations run before the application release that depends on them, in a separate step, so that a migration failure does not leave a half deployed release. The migration console reports each migration as pending, applied, or failed.

## Inverse Migrations

Every migration must ship with an inverse migration, but an inverse is not applied automatically during a rollback. Application rollback and migration rollback are separate operations on purpose: reverting a schema change under live traffic is far riskier than reverting an application image, and doing it automatically would make a routine rollback a data risk.

To revert a schema change, roll the application back first, confirm it is healthy, and then apply the inverse migration from the migration console. Applying an inverse while the newer application version is still serving traffic will cause write failures.

## Forward Incompatible Migrations

A migration is forward incompatible when the previous application version cannot run against the new schema. Forward incompatible migrations must be split into an expand step and a contract step released at least one version apart, so that a rollback target always exists.

A migration that has been applied for more than fourteen days cannot be inverted from the console, because the fourteen day artifact window means the application version that preceded it may no longer be deployable.

documents.title: Meridian Artifact and Object Storage
documents.text:
# Meridian Artifact and Object Storage

## Build Artifacts

Build artifacts are container images produced by the release pipeline and stored in the artifact registry. An artifact is retained in the registry for fourteen days, after which it is garbage collected. This fourteen day window is what makes a rollback older than fourteen days fail with a registry miss.

Garbage collected artifacts are not lost. They are moved to cold storage and are retained there for one year. Restoring an artifact from cold storage takes roughly eight minutes and is done with the artifact restore command.

## Workspace Objects

Workspace objects are customer content and follow the data retention policy rather than the artifact policy. They are not garbage collected on the fourteen day cycle, and the two windows are unrelated despite both being described as retention.

## Backups

Backups of the primary database are taken hourly and are retained on a ninety day cycle. A backup is a point in time copy and cannot be restored into a running cluster; restoring one provisions a new cluster and then cuts over, which takes approximately forty minutes.

Backups are encrypted under the account key version current at the time the backup was written, so restoring a backup older than the key retention window requires the key restore procedure first.

documents.title: Meridian Directory Provisioning
documents.text:
# Meridian Directory Provisioning

## Provisioning Model

Meridian synchronises user accounts from an external directory using directory provisioning. Provisioning creates, updates, and deactivates Meridian accounts to match the directory; it does not handle sign in. Authentication remains the responsibility of Meridian's own token system.

A provisioned account cannot change its own email address or display name in Meridian, because the next synchronisation would overwrite the change. Attempting to do so returns a directory managed response.

## Synchronisation

Synchronisation runs every four hours, and an account owner may trigger it manually once per hour. A synchronisation that would deactivate more than ten percent of accounts in a single run is halted and flagged for confirmation, because that pattern usually indicates a misconfigured directory filter rather than a genuine bulk departure.

Deactivation through provisioning revokes session tokens immediately. It does not revoke workspace tokens or service tokens, which are account scoped rather than user scoped and must be revoked separately.

## Group Mapping

Directory groups map to Meridian workspace roles through an explicit mapping table. Unmapped groups are ignored rather than defaulting to a role, so that adding a group in the directory never silently grants access in Meridian.

documents.title: Meridian CLI Error Reference
documents.text:
# Meridian CLI Error Reference

## Error Codes

The Meridian CLI reports failures with a stable error code. Error codes are never reused, and a code retired from the CLI is left documented rather than removed.

Error E1042 means the release tag was not found in the artifact registry. It is most often produced by a rollback to a tag older than the fourteen day artifact window, and is resolved by restoring the artifact from cold storage first.

Error E2071 means the migration console refused an inverse migration because the migration is older than fourteen days.

Error E3310 means the supplied token does not carry the scope required by the command. This is a scope failure and not an expiry failure; an expired token reports E3311 instead.

Error E4021 means a write was rejected because the workspace is at its storage quota. It is not a rate limit error; rate limiting reports E4200 with a retry after value.

## Exit Codes

The CLI exits zero on success, one on a user error such as a bad argument, two on an authentication or scope failure, and three on a server error. A rate limited request exits three rather than one, because it is a transient server side condition rather than a mistake by the caller.

## Diagnostics

The meridian diagnose command collects the CLI version, the resolved account and workspace, the last ten requests with their error codes, and the local clock skew. Clock skew above sixty seconds is reported prominently, because token validation failures caused by skew otherwise look like scope failures.

documents.title: Meridian Webhooks
documents.text:
# Meridian Webhooks

## Delivery

A Meridian webhook delivers an event to a customer endpoint over HTTPS. Delivery is at least once, not exactly once, so an endpoint must be idempotent. Each delivery carries an event id that is stable across retries, which is what an endpoint should deduplicate on.

A delivery is considered successful when the endpoint returns any two hundred level response within ten seconds. A slower response is treated as a failure even if it eventually arrives.

## Retries

A failed delivery is retried with exponential backoff at one minute, five minutes, thirty minutes, two hours, and finally six hours. After the fifth failed attempt the delivery is dropped and the endpoint is marked degraded.

Webhook retries are unrelated to API rate limiting. A rate limited API caller is told to retry with a retry after header; a failed webhook delivery is retried by Meridian on the schedule above without any action from the customer.

An endpoint that is marked degraded for more than seven consecutive days is disabled, and the account owner is notified. A disabled endpoint must be re-enabled manually, and re-enabling does not replay the dropped deliveries.

## Signing

Every delivery is signed with a webhook signing secret, which is distinct from any token type. The signing secret is displayed once at creation and can be rotated with an overlap period of twenty four hours, during which both the old and new signatures are accepted.

documents.title: Meridian Logs and Metrics
documents.text:
# Meridian Logs and Metrics

## Log Streams

Meridian exposes three log streams. The request log records one entry per API request with the token type, the workspace, and the response status. The audit log records administrative actions such as token creation, role changes, and deletion requests. The application log records internal diagnostics and is not customer visible.

The request log is retained for thirty days, matching the application log window. The audit log is retained for four hundred days, because it is the record used for compliance review.

## Log Rotation

Log files rotate hourly on the collector and are compressed after rotation. Log rotation is a storage mechanism and has nothing to do with token rotation or encryption key rotation, despite the shared word; the three are frequently confused in support requests.

## Metrics

Metrics are emitted at one minute resolution and are downsampled to five minute resolution after seven days and to one hour resolution after ninety days. Downsampled metrics keep minimum, maximum, and average, so a spike remains visible after downsampling even though its exact shape does not.

## Alerts

An alert fires against a metric threshold sustained over a window rather than against a single sample, because one minute resolution makes single sample alerts unusably noisy. An alert that fires during a declared deploy freeze is still delivered but is tagged with the freeze, so that a reviewer can tell an expected alert from an unexpected one.

queries.reference: Yes. Both signatures are accepted during a twenty four hour overlap.

queries.query: When a user is deactivated in the directory, are their automation tokens revoked?
queries.reference: No. Only session tokens are revoked; workspace and service tokens are account scoped.
